item.title: A Raspberry Pi MS-DOS Build
item.description:
Introduction

As a ‘young’ Millennial, I grew up in the late 90s and early 2000s. Even then, for a variety of reasons, my family often lagged a generation behind on tech. As such, I grew up on late MS-DOS games alongside early Windows games, and due to nostalgia and my growing interest in the fundamental ways computers work, I’ve developed a greater interest in retro computers and games.

Over the early months of 2026, I also found myself developing an interest in single-board computers (Raspberry Pi) and microcontrollers, but I needed a basic project that I could start off with, so I decided to give this a try. I really want to get into retro computing proper, but it’s not a cheap hobby by any means. Instead, I decided to combine these two recent interests as a starter Pi project and build a “nostalgia box” to relive some level of my early childhood experiences on PC!

item.title: An Unnecessarily Complicated Framework: my blog pipeline
item.description:
If you’re reading this blog, chances are that you don’t realize how complicated things are behind the scenes. What looks like a visually-appealing, easy-to-view blog for my career, home lab and tech opinions is actually several Git(hub) repositories publishing markdown files piped in direct from my primary Obsidian vault.

Why did I do it this way, when spinning up something like a WordPress blog would’ve been so much simpler and easier?

item.title: Network Nightmare [Troubleshooting Tales #1]
item.description: In over eight months of using Manjaro Linux as my daily driver, I’ve encountered a handful of oddities and issues that I’ve had to sink a few hours into fixing. By and large, the experience has been smooth, but when something breaks, it seems to break randomly and without immediately apparent cause. I just dealt with another such situation and figured I would write down what I did to fix the issue as part of a new post series I’m starting: “Troubleshooting Tales”.
